description: How diet causes or prevents obesity, CVD, bone disease, dental decay, anaemia and type 2 diabetes.
content_html:
The Link Between Diet and Health

What you eat does not only affect your weight — it shapes your long-term risk of several serious conditions. The written paper expects you to explain these relationships as cause-and-effect chains, not just lists. For every condition below, you need to know: which dietary factors increase the risk, what happens in the body as a result, and what dietary changes reduce the risk. Starting with a clear chain — “high saturated fat intake raises LDL cholesterol, which builds up in artery walls, narrowing them, which raises the risk of heart attack” — is far more valuable than a list of “foods to avoid”.

Obesity

Obesity results from sustained positive energy balance — eating more calories than the body uses — so the excess energy is stored as body fat. Dietary risk factors include: a diet high in energy-dense foods (those rich in fat and/or free sugars); large portion sizes; frequent consumption of processed snack foods, fast food and sugary drinks; and low intake of fibre (which promotes satiety). Obesity raises the risk of type 2 diabetes, coronary heart disease, certain cancers, osteoarthritis and mental health difficulties. Dietary modifications to prevent or reduce obesity: reduce energy-dense foods; increase fibre (promotes fullness); increase fruit and vegetables; choose leaner cooking methods (grill or steam rather than deep-fry); reduce alcohol (which is energy-dense but nutrient-poor); control portion sizes.

Cardiovascular Health — CHD and High Blood Pressure

Coronary heart disease (CHD) develops when the coronary arteries supplying the heart become narrowed or blocked. The key dietary chain is: a high intake of saturated fats raises the level of LDL (“bad”) cholesterol in the blood. Over time, LDL cholesterol deposits form plaques on the artery walls (a process called atherosclerosis), narrowing the arteries. A narrowed coronary artery reduces blood flow to the heart, which can cause angina (chest pain) or, if a clot blocks the artery completely, a heart attack.

Hypertension (high blood pressure) is independently linked to a high sodium (salt) intake. Excess salt causes the body to retain water, increasing blood volume and pressure against artery walls. High blood pressure damages artery walls, speeding up atherosclerosis and raising the risk of stroke and heart failure. The maximum recommended adult intake is 6 g of salt (2.4 g sodium) per day; most UK adults exceed this because processed foods, bread and ready meals are the main contributors.

Key Fact

High saturated fat → raises LDL cholesterol → atherosclerosis (plaque build-up in artery walls) → narrowed coronary arteries → reduced blood flow to the heart → angina or heart attack. High salt intake → raised blood pressure (hypertension) → increased risk of stroke and CHD.

Many students write only that a “bad diet causes obesity and then disease”, and stop there. This misses several independent dietary links. A person of healthy weight can still develop CHD from a diet high in saturated fat (because LDL cholesterol rises regardless of BMI). A slim person can develop iron-deficiency anaemia if they avoid red meat, fortified cereals and vitamin-C-rich foods. A child of any weight can develop rickets if their diet is low in vitamin D and calcium. The exam rewards students who can explain each disease through its own specific dietary mechanism, not just through obesity as an intermediate step.

Bone Health — Rickets and Osteoporosis

Bones need calcium and vitamin D to develop and stay strong. Without adequate calcium, the body draws calcium from bones to maintain blood levels, gradually weakening them. Without vitamin D, calcium cannot be absorbed from the gut, so even a calcium-rich diet does not fully protect bones if vitamin D is deficient.

  • Rickets (in children) — caused by deficiency of vitamin D and/or calcium. The leg bones soften and bow outwards because they cannot mineralise properly. Dietary sources of vitamin D include oily fish, eggs and fortified foods; sunlight exposure also triggers skin synthesis. Risk groups: children in the UK who have limited sun exposure, especially in winter.
  • Osteoporosis (in adults) — gradual loss of bone density, making bones fragile and prone to fracture. Risk factors include a long-term low-calcium diet, vitamin D deficiency, low oestrogen (after the menopause in women), smoking and physical inactivity. Peak bone mass is reached in the early twenties, so calcium and vitamin D intake during childhood and adolescence directly affects long-term osteoporosis risk.

Dental Health

Tooth decay (dental caries) occurs when bacteria in the mouth ferment sugars to produce acids, which dissolve tooth enamel. Frequent consumption of free sugars — particularly between meals, when saliva flow is lower — increases the time teeth are exposed to acid attack. Sugary drinks, sweets, biscuits, cakes and fruit juices are the main culprits. Fluoride strengthens tooth enamel and increases its resistance to acid, which is why fluoridated water and fluoride toothpaste are public health measures. Calcium and phosphorus in dairy products help remineralise enamel. Reducing the frequency and amount of free sugar consumed is the most effective dietary strategy to protect dental health.

Iron-Deficiency Anaemia

Iron-deficiency anaemia develops when the body does not have enough iron to make adequate haemoglobin. Haemoglobin is the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen to every tissue; when levels are low, the body cannot supply enough oxygen, causing tiredness, pale skin, breathlessness and poor concentration. Risk groups: teenage girls and adult women (menstrual losses); pregnant women (iron demand rises to support the fetus and placenta); young children (rapid growth increases demand); and people following vegetarian or vegan diets (plant sources of iron are less well absorbed). Dietary strategies: eat iron-rich foods (red meat, liver, oily fish, fortified cereals, lentils, dark green vegetables); eat these alongside vitamin C (orange juice, pepper, tomato) to enhance non-haem iron absorption; avoid drinking tea with meals (tannins in tea inhibit iron absorption).

Key Fact

Iron-deficiency anaemia risk groups: teenage girls, adult women, pregnant women, young children, vegetarians and vegans. Eating iron-rich foods alongside vitamin C increases absorption of non-haem iron from plant sources. Tea at mealtimes reduces iron absorption.

Type 2 Diabetes

Type 2 diabetes occurs when the body becomes resistant to insulin or cannot produce enough insulin to keep blood glucose at a normal level. After eating, blood glucose rises; insulin is released by the pancreas to move glucose into cells for energy. In type 2 diabetes, cells become less responsive to insulin (insulin resistance), and blood glucose remains elevated. Over time, high blood glucose damages blood vessels and nerves, increasing the risk of heart disease, kidney failure, blindness and amputations.

The main dietary risk factors for type 2 diabetes are: obesity (excess body fat, especially around the abdomen, is strongly associated with insulin resistance); a high intake of refined carbohydrates and free sugars (which cause rapid spikes in blood glucose, repeatedly demanding high insulin output); and low dietary fibre intake (fibre slows glucose absorption, reducing blood glucose spikes). Dietary management after diagnosis: reduce free sugars and refined carbohydrates; choose low-glycaemic-index foods (wholegrain bread, oats, lentils, pulses); increase dietary fibre; control portion sizes; lose weight if overweight to improve insulin sensitivity.

These are the chains the exam tests most often:

  • CHD: high saturated fat → raised LDL cholesterol → atherosclerosis → narrowed arteries → heart attack.
  • Hypertension: high salt intake → fluid retention → raised blood pressure → stroke/CHD.
  • Type 2 diabetes: excess free sugars and refined carbs + obesity → insulin resistance → chronic raised blood glucose → damage to blood vessels and nerves.
  • Anaemia: low iron intake (or poor absorption) → insufficient haemoglobin → reduced oxygen delivery → fatigue and pale skin.
  • Dental decay: frequent free sugar intake → bacterial fermentation → acid attack on enamel → tooth decay.
  • Rickets/osteoporosis: low vitamin D and/or calcium → poor bone mineralisation → soft bones (children) or fragile bones (adults).
exam_tip_html: The most common error on diet-related disease questions is describing rather than analysing. Describe means “give an account including all relevant characteristics” — so naming the disease and one dietary cause earns marks. Explain means “give reasons for and/or causes of” — so you must use ‘because’, ‘this means that’ and ‘as a result’ to build a chain. For the 9-mark Analyse capstone, you are expected to break the topic into parts and examine the relationships between them. For example, if asked to analyse how dietary changes can manage type 2 diabetes: (1) analyse the role of refined carbohydrates in blood glucose spikes and insulin demand; (2) analyse how dietary fibre reduces glucose absorption rate; (3) analyse the link between weight loss and improved insulin sensitivity. Each part must be examined for its relationship to the others, not described in isolation. For 12-mark Evaluate questions, always reach a supported judgement — state clearly which dietary change is most important and why, using named technical terms.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Diet-related diseases are caused by specific dietary mechanisms, not just “poor diet”. Learn each cause-and-effect chain: high saturated fat and CHD; high salt and hypertension; low vitamin D/calcium and rickets/osteoporosis; frequent free sugars and dental decay; low iron and anaemia; excess free sugars with obesity and type 2 diabetes.
  • Iron-deficiency anaemia is most common in teenage girls, pregnant women and vegans. Eating iron-rich foods with vitamin C boosts absorption; tea at mealtimes reduces it.
  • Type 2 diabetes develops when cells become resistant to insulin, often driven by a diet high in refined carbohydrates and free sugars combined with obesity. Dietary management focuses on low-GI foods, increased fibre, reduced free sugars and weight management.

practice_questions.text:
Which condition is caused by a long-term deficiency of both vitamin D and calcium in children?
A. Iron-deficiency anaemia
B. Rickets
C. Type 2 diabetes
D. Dental caries
State two dietary changes a person with high blood pressure could make to lower their risk.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any two of: reduce salt/sodium intake; reduce saturated fat intake; increase fruit and vegetable intake; increase dietary fibre; reduce alcohol intake; eat oily fish for omega-3 fatty acids; use herbs and spices instead of salt when cooking. Maximum 2 marks.

practice_questions.text: Describe how a diet high in free sugars can lead to dental decay.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any three accurate, distinct points: bacteria in the mouth ferment free sugars; this produces acids; the acids dissolve (demineralise) tooth enamel; frequent consumption (especially between meals) means teeth are repeatedly exposed to acid attacks; the protective effect of saliva is reduced between meals; over time, holes (cavities/dental caries) form in the enamel. Up to 3 marks.

practice_questions.text: Fatima is a 17-year-old vegetarian who is often tired, has pale skin and struggles to concentrate at school. Her GP suspects iron-deficiency anaemia. Explain why Fatima may be at risk and identify two dietary strategies that could help.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks. 2 marks per developed explanation. (1) Risk: Fatima follows a vegetarian diet, which typically provides only non-haem iron from plant sources (lentils, spinach, fortified cereals) rather than the more easily absorbed haem iron from red meat; non-haem iron has lower bioavailability, meaning her body absorbs a smaller proportion of the iron she eats; she may also have higher iron needs because of menstrual losses. (2) Strategies: eat iron-rich plant foods (fortified cereals, dark green vegetables, lentils, beans) alongside a source of vitamin C (orange juice, fresh tomatoes, peppers), because vitamin C converts non-haem iron into a more readily absorbed form; avoid drinking tea or coffee with meals, as tannins inhibit iron absorption. 1 mark for identification of risk mechanism; 1 mark for developed consequence or specific strategy per point.

practice_questions.text: Describe the main dietary risk factors for developing type 2 diabetes.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any three accurate points: high intake of refined carbohydrates and/or free sugars (causing repeated blood glucose spikes and high insulin demand, leading to insulin resistance over time); obesity or excess body fat (especially abdominal fat is strongly linked to insulin resistance); low dietary fibre intake (fibre slows glucose absorption and helps regulate blood glucose levels); large portion sizes and a high-calorie diet that promotes weight gain. Up to 3 marks.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the dietary changes a person newly diagnosed with type 2 diabetes should make to manage their condition, considering both short-term blood glucose control and long-term health outcomes.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10–12 marks): Evaluates dietary changes under at least two dimensions (short-term BG control AND long-term outcomes), using specific, accurate dietary advice and linking it to the underlying mechanisms. Short-term: reducing free sugars and refined carbohydrates reduces blood glucose spikes and lowers the demand on the pancreas to release insulin, helping to prevent hyperglycaemia; increasing dietary fibre (wholegrain bread, oats, pulses) slows glucose absorption so the rise in blood glucose after meals is gentler. Long-term: managing body weight through calorie reduction and increased fibre intake improves insulin sensitivity, which is the central problem in type 2 diabetes; reducing saturated fat lowers CHD risk (people with type 2 diabetes are at higher risk of cardiovascular disease); adequate calcium and vitamin D protect bones (some diabetes medications can affect bone density). JUDGEMENT: explicitly weighs the relative importance of changes (e.g. 'Reducing free sugars and losing weight are the highest-priority changes because they directly address insulin resistance — the root cause — whereas fat and micronutrient management, while valuable, address secondary complications.'). Accurate use of insulin resistance, blood glucose, glycaemic index, dietary fibre, LDL cholesterol and atherosclerosis throughout.

Secure (7–9 marks): Addresses both short-term glucose control and at least one long-term consideration. Reaches a partial judgement. Mostly accurate, with some applied vocabulary.

Developing (4–6 marks): Describes dietary changes without sustained evaluation of both time horizons; judgement weak or absent; one-sided or mainly descriptive.

Emerging (1–3 marks): Basic points about eating less sugar with no development of mechanism, application to the person, or comparison of the importance of different changes.

knowledge_checks.q: Which sequence correctly describes the dietary pathway from high saturated fat intake to coronary heart disease?
options: High saturated fat → low HDL → blood clot → heart attack
High saturated fat → raised LDL cholesterol → atherosclerosis → narrowed coronary arteries
High saturated fat → raised blood glucose → insulin resistance → heart disease
High saturated fat → calcium loss from bones → brittle arteries → heart disease

knowledge_checks.q: Which nutrient, when consumed alongside plant-based iron-rich foods, significantly increases non-haem iron absorption?
Osteoporosis is a condition in which gradual loss of _____ density makes bones fragile and prone to fracture in adults.
In type 2 diabetes, cells become resistant to _____, meaning blood glucose cannot be moved into cells efficiently and remains elevated.
Match each diet-related condition with its primary dietary risk factor.
right: Frequent free sugar intake providing fuel for acid-producing bacteria
Low iron intake or poor iron absorption from plant-only diets
High sodium (salt) intake causing fluid retention and raised blood pressure

flashcard_questions.q: What is obesity and what is its primary dietary cause?
flashcard_questions.a: Excess body fat caused by sustained positive energy balance — eating more energy than is expended.

flashcard_questions.q: How does a high saturated fat intake increase the risk of coronary heart disease?
flashcard_questions.a: It raises LDL cholesterol, which builds up as plaque in artery walls (atherosclerosis), narrowing the coronary arteries.

flashcard_questions.q: How does high salt intake raise blood pressure?
flashcard_questions.a: Excess sodium causes the body to retain water, increasing blood volume and pressure on artery walls.

flashcard_questions.q: What bone condition in children is caused by vitamin D and calcium deficiency?
flashcard_questions.a: Rickets — the leg bones soften and bow because they cannot mineralise properly.

flashcard_questions.q: What is osteoporosis and when does risk increase?
flashcard_questions.a: Loss of bone density making bones fragile; risk rises after the menopause and with a lifetime of low calcium intake.
Insufficient haemoglobin due to low iron, reducing the blood's ability to carry oxygen and causing fatigue.

flashcard_questions.q: Why does tea at mealtimes reduce iron absorption?
flashcard_questions.a: Tannins in tea bind to non-haem iron and prevent it from being absorbed in the gut.

flashcard_questions.q: What happens to blood glucose in type 2 diabetes?
flashcard_questions.a: Cells become resistant to insulin, so blood glucose remains elevated after meals.

flashcard_questions.q: How does dietary fibre help manage blood glucose levels in type 2 diabetes?
flashcard_questions.a: Fibre slows the absorption of glucose from the gut, reducing blood glucose spikes after eating.

flashcard_questions.q: How does dental caries develop from a high free-sugar diet?
flashcard_questions.a: Bacteria ferment sugars, producing acids that dissolve tooth enamel over repeated exposures.

flashcard_questions.q: Name two dietary measures to reduce the risk of osteoporosis.
flashcard_questions.a: Adequate calcium intake and adequate vitamin D (from oily fish, eggs, fortified foods and sunlight).

flashcard_questions.q: Which dietary change most directly addresses insulin resistance in type 2 diabetes?
flashcard_questions.a: Reducing free sugars and refined carbohydrates, and losing weight to improve insulin sensitivity.

glossary_terms.definition: A condition in which excess body fat has accumulated to the extent that it may have an adverse effect on health, typically measured using body mass index (BMI).
Fats that are solid at room temperature and found mainly in animal products; excess intake raises LDL cholesterol levels in the blood.
The build-up of fatty plaques inside artery walls, causing narrowing that restricts blood flow and increases the risk of heart attack and stroke.
A condition in which a lack of iron leads to insufficient haemoglobin, reducing the blood's ability to carry oxygen and causing fatigue, pale skin and breathlessness.
A metabolic condition in which the body either does not produce enough insulin or does not respond to it effectively, leading to elevated blood glucose levels.
Persistently raised blood pressure in the arteries, linked to a high salt intake and increased risk of stroke and coronary heart disease.
